# Multiple Predictors {#lm-multiple-predictors}

<div class="draft">Work in progress.</div>

Placeholder for a later chapter. Ideas so far:

- Chapters \@ref(lm-mean) to \@ref(lm-one-way-anova) use one predictor each; most real questions involve more than one
- `lm(y ~ a + b)`: each slope is the effect of one predictor with the others held fixed
- factorial ANOVA as multiple regression
  - two categorical predictors, each dummy coded as in Chapter \@ref(lm-one-way-anova)
  - interaction = product of the dummy columns; `lm(y ~ a * b)` is shorthand for `a + b + a:b`
  - same F-values as the factorial ANOVA in Chapter \@ref(factorial-anova); check against `aov()`
  - unbalanced groups: the order of predictors changes the sums of squares (Type I vs Type II/III); short note only
- ANCOVA as multiple regression
  - one categorical predictor plus one continuous covariate: `lm(y ~ group + covariate)`
  - group difference "adjusted" for the covariate = the group slope with the covariate held fixed
  - possible example: `iris` sepal length vs sepal width, r = -.12 overall but positive within each species (Simpson's paradox); adding `Species` flips the sign of the slope
- multiple regression with continuous predictors
  - no classic named test it reduces to, unlike the t-test or ANOVA
  - nearest links: each slope's t-test is the same as the test of a partial correlation; the overall F compares the model with the mean-only model (Chapter \@ref(lm-mean)), as in Chapter \@ref(lm-one-way-anova)
  - R-squared: share of the variance the predictors explain together
- outcomes that are not continuous (yes/no, counts): see the generalised and mixed models book
